e.etymology: A modern American coinage built from the Jan- of Janiyah and Janelle with the -ylah ending heard in Jaylah and Nylah.
A clipped form of Ezekiel, from Hebrew Yehezkel, God strengthens, the name of the Old Testament prophet. Dropping the first vowel puts the nickname Zeke up front.
From Anglo-Norman fitz, son, from Latin filius. It opens surnames such as Fitzgerald and Fitzpatrick, and serves as a short form of them or as a name on its own.
namesakes: Fitzgerald Grant, called Fitz (president on TV's Scandal)

e.etymology: A respelling of Maisie, the Scottish pet form of Margaret by way of Gaelic Mairead. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, pearl.
A modern American coinage that joins the De- prefix to the -kari ending heard in Dakari, Jakari and Zakari.
A respelling of Hazel, from the English word for the hazel tree and its light brown color, Old English haesel.

assoc.t: hazel, the green-brown eye color and the nut tree

e.etymology: From the Arabic root z-y-n, beauty and adornment, the same root as Zayn. The doubled-a spelling is the usual one among South Asian Muslim families.
A pet form of Esther, also of Estelle and Estella. Esther is usually traced to a Persian word for star, and Estelle to Latin stella, star.
The Spanish, Scandinavian and Polish spelling of Jonathan, from Hebrew Yehonatan, the Lord has given. In the Bible Jonathan is King Saul's son and David's loyal friend.
From the English word amity, friendship, which came through Old French amitié from Latin amicus, friend. It belongs with virtue names like Verity and Felicity.

assoc.t: Amity Island, the beach town in Jaws
Amity Blight in Disney's The Owl House
Amity, the peaceful faction in Divergent

e.etymology: A modern American name, a spelling in the Kamiyah and Kamaya family that joins Ka- to Miah. It also matches Kamiah, an Idaho town whose name comes from the Nez Perce language.
A form of Aurea, from Latin aureus, golden. Auria was used in medieval Spain, where an 11th-century saint is known as Aurea or Oria; today it also reads as a cousin of Aurelia and Aura.
A surname, in Germany tied to the town of Witten in the Ruhr valley. American parents took it up as a first name in the 2010s, when Jason Witten was the Dallas Cowboys' star tight end.

e.meaning: of the forest, or asked for
e.etymology: A respelling of Silas, Paul's companion in the Book of Acts. He is also called Silvanus, a Latin name from silva, forest; Silas may itself be an Aramaic form of Saul, asked for.
A modern American coinage in the Aniyah family, with the -lah ending heard in Nylah and Jaylah.
From Latin prosperus, fortunate, the name of a 5th-century saint, Prosper of Aquitaine. It came into English through French, and the English verb prosper keeps the sense plain.

assoc.t: Prosper, Texas, a fast-growing Dallas suburb

e.etymology: A modern blend of Ana with Laya or Alaya, close in sound to Analia and Anaya.
e.note: The first four letters spell anal, an opening for teasing; the spelling Annalaya avoids it.

e.etymology: From an English surname for a guard or watchman, Old English weard. It has also served as a short form of Edward and Howard.
namesakes: Ward Cleaver (the father on Leave It to Beaver)

assoc.t: ward, as in a hospital ward or a ward of the court

e.etymology: A modern elaboration of Jane or Jay, in the pattern of Dayna and Shayna. Jayna is also the female Wonder Twin in the Super Friends cartoons of the 1970s.

assoc.t: Jayna of the Wonder Twins in DC's Super Friends

e.etymology: A spelling of Stephanie, the French feminine of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, crown or wreath. The f spelling is common among Spanish-speaking families.
From Hebrew Yedidyah, beloved of the Lord. In 2 Samuel the prophet Nathan gives it as a second, blessing name to the infant Solomon. Jedidiah is the older English spelling.
namesakes: Jedediah Smith (19th-century mountain man and explorer of the West)

e.etymology: One of a cluster of modern names, with Janeli, Yaneli and Yanely, favored by Hispanic families in the United States. Its source is unclear, though it sits close to Janelle and Jane.
A form of Aryan or Arian, from the ancient Indo-Iranian word arya, noble, the source of the name Iran. It is used in Iran and across South Asia.
e.note: Close to Aryan, a word many Americans link with Nazi racial ideology; this spelling softens the echo without removing it.

e.etymology: From Arabic subhan, glory or praise, familiar from the phrase subhan Allah, glory be to God. As a name it is most common in Pakistan and Bangladesh.
A modern American coinage that puts the Za- opening on Alaya or Laya, in the pattern of Zaniyah and Zariyah.
Made familiar by the singer and Empire actress Serayah. It echoes Seraiah, a Hebrew name borne by several men in the Old Testament, and sits near Saraya and Soraya in sound.
namesakes: Serayah (singer and actress on Fox's Empire)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that stretches Ace with an -en ending, so that it rhymes with Mason and Jason.
From ajuni in the Mool Mantar, the opening verse of the Sikh scripture, where it describes God as unborn, outside the cycle of birth and death. It is a Sikh name, given mostly to girls.
A pet form of Laura and Lauren for girls and of Laurence for boys, all from Latin laurus, the laurel tree whose leaves crowned victors. It was a top American girls' name around 1960.
namesakes: Laurie Metcalf (actress in Roseanne and Lady Bird)
Laurie Strode (heroine of the Halloween films)

assoc.t: Laurie, the boy next door in Little Women

e.etymology: A spelling of Laura, from Latin laurus, the laurel tree; Petrarch's sonnets to Laura made the name famous. Lora has also served as a short form of Eleonora and Lorraine.
A short form of names ending in -ina, such as Christina, Georgina and Wilhelmina, used on its own since the 1800s.
namesakes: Ina Garten (Barefoot Contessa cookbook author and TV host)
e.note: Americans usually say EYE-nuh, as Ina Garten does; in Germany and Scandinavia it is EE-nah.

assoc.t: Ina Garten, the Barefoot Contessa TV cook

e.etymology: The medieval English form of Juliana, the feminine of Julian, from the Roman family name Julius. It was so common that Jill became a byword for a girl, and it was revived in 20th-century Britain.
namesakes: Gillian Anderson (actress, The X-Files and The Crown)
e.note: The British sometimes use a hard G; Americans say JIL-ee-un, and the spelling Jillian avoids the question.
